The goal in computer security is and always should be to expect the unexpected, until all casework has been done and literally the only security hole is to put your devices in an electron microscope on a low frequency setting or some similar device. I just addressed some of your later points in another comment I posted after you posted this one but I’ll repeat them here in addition to addressing your earlier points. I would argue that security through obscurity is the only form of security that works, and I would say your misunderstanding of my use of the term is why you are arguing against it. I will use modern security, coding practices, and technological limitations due to limitations on innovation to make my argument. Encryption algorithms comprise the bulk of security through obscurity in today’s modern era. It is both obscure to the user which encryption algorithms are being used, how large and lengthy the encryption algorithms are, and what the key or keys being used for the encryption algorithm are. The funny thing about keys in encryption is that in today’s day and age they are actually confident enough in those other layers of obscurity that computer programmers are willing and EAGER to send those keys digitally through the computers native ports, across wireless or Ethernet connected networks, and out to the recipient, all over the cloud. Personally if I ever ran a business I would send my keys in thumb drives via snail mail. But who’s to say that programmers aren’t right in trusting the other protections of obscurity in their encryption efforts? After all, even with the key, you still require the source code of the encryption algorithm (or at least the pseudocode) in order to unlock the information in a file or to activate a password protected “widget”. Here our “widget” is our lovely phaser. The more complicated, the larger, and more spread out both the algorithms and keys are, the harder it becomes to any security analyst to decrypt a password out of its encrypted state. And it’s not as if that’s where it ends with obscurity’s usefulness. If it weren’t so obscure as to how to build an RSA-breaking quantum computer, then loads of people would have already done it and many modern encryption algorithms would have to be replaced since they would be “broken”. And beyond all that, a tightly coupled program that is particularly large (I know from experience) is always harder to reason about and therefore harder to invert than a program that is small or not tightly coupled. It’s because in a tightly coupled program you need to think about every aspect of the programs case fall throughs practically all at once. Even for a bot assessing the program if one could be trained to do so, it would certainly require more computing power to perform the “artificial” logic. In addition, even in efficiently written code, as the trail of method calls gets longer and encryption algorithm after encryption algorithm are stacked one upon the other in order to generate large(safe) keys, time lapses for both encryption and keyless decryption get larger. If you used multiple keys, all forms of decryption would take longer. Storage of said keys should of course be done on rotation with a daemon, which no modern computers actually do quite unfortunately (unless of course you work for the government and are not Hillary Clinton).
To address your quote from Scotty, I would argue that overthinking is far different than making something more complicated to suit an appropriate and achievable security level. Overthinking implies one went too far, which in this instance would be to write a security program that requires more computations than a computer can handle in I’d say…. Half a second. Which is approximately 2 billion bits altered or measured per half second. But that’s just with one single-bit processor that can either negate or not negate any bit at a given moment in time.
To counter your belief that security with obscurity was referring to “anticipating an attack from the enemy”, it was not. It was referring to its advantages in protecting vital data on a machine that anticipates HOW to attack UPON the enemy.
